topic: Returning to exercise after pregnancy

slides.headline: Exercise after baby: where to start
slides.sub: A gentle, realistic way back to movement after pregnancy.

slides.title: Start with a check-in
slides.body: Most people have a postnatal check with their GP or care team around six weeks. It's a good time to ask about returning to exercise, especially after a caesarean or a difficult birth.

slides.title: Pelvic floor first
slides.body: Pelvic floor exercises can usually start early, gently and often lying down. Think squeeze and lift, then fully relax. Building these up before higher-impact exercise is a sensible starting point.

slides.title: Gentle walks and breathing
slides.body: Short walks, deep breathing and gentle core work are common early steps. Build time and intensity gradually. Sleep is patchy, so small and regular often works better than long and occasional.

slides.title: Tummy gap is common
slides.body: Some separation of the tummy muscles after pregnancy is normal and often improves over time. A clinician can check it and guide exercises that load your core gradually and comfortably.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Leaking, a feeling of heaviness or dragging in the pelvis, pain during exercise, heavy bleeding or a wound that isn't healing. Talk to your GP or a women's health physio.

slides.headline: Ready to rebuild, gently?
slides.body: Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy assesses first, then builds sessions around your recovery and goals. Check with your fund about cover.

caption:
Wondering when and how to get moving again after having a baby?

A good first step is your postnatal check with your GP or care team, often around six weeks. From there, most people start with pelvic floor exercises, short walks, breathing and gentle core work, then build up gradually before returning to running or higher-impact training.

Some tummy muscle separation is normal after pregnancy and often improves. Leaking, pelvic heaviness, pain during exercise or heavy bleeding is worth raising with your GP or a women's health physio.

topic: Why your scan report sounds scarier than it is

slides.headline: Scan report sounds terrifying?
slides.sub: Why the words are usually scarier than what they mean.

slides.title: Reports are written for doctors
slides.body: Radiologists describe everything they see, in precise medical language. That's their job. It isn't a list of problems causing your pain, and many findings are simply normal features of a body that has lived a few decades.

slides.title: Common findings in pain-less backs
slides.body: Research suggests disc bulges, dehydrated discs and joint changes show up often in scans of people with no pain at all. They become more common with age, a bit like grey hair on the inside.

slides.title: Translating a few scary words
slides.body: 'Degenerative' usually means age-related. 'Bulge' means the disc sits slightly past its usual edge. A disc 'tear' often describes a small fissure seen in many people. None of these automatically means fragile.

slides.title: What matters more than the picture
slides.body: How your pain behaves, what you can and can't do, your sleep, stress and activity levels. These usually guide the plan far more than the scan, and many people improve heaps with the same result.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Worsening leg weakness, numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, fever, unexplained weight loss or pain after a big fall need prompt medical review. These are uncommon, and your GP or physio can guide you.

slides.headline: Bring the report, we'll talk it through
slides.body: Our Sunnybank and Milton physios explain what your scan does and doesn't mean, then build a plan around how you move. Book online, link in bio.

caption:
Read your scan report and felt your stomach drop? You're not alone.

Scan reports are written by radiologists for other clinicians. They list everything visible, in precise language, and words like "degenerative", "bulge" or "tear" sound far worse than they usually are. Research suggests many of these findings are common in people with no pain at all, and they become more common with age.

What usually matters more is how your pain behaves, what you can do, and your sleep, stress and activity levels. A few things do need prompt review: worsening leg weakness, numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, fever or unexplained weight loss.

Our Sunnybank and Milton physios can go through your report with you in plain English and build a plan around how you move. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: Massage for tension headaches

slides.headline: Headache that starts in your neck?
slides.sub: What remedial massage can and can't do for tension headaches.

slides.title: What a tension headache feels like
slides.body: Often a band-like pressure across the forehead or the back of the head, on both sides, dull rather than throbbing. Many people notice tight, tender neck and shoulder muscles alongside it.

slides.title: Where massage can help
slides.body: Remedial massage to the neck, upper shoulders and base of the skull can ease muscle tenderness and help you feel less tense. Research suggests it may reduce how often some people get these headaches.

slides.title: What it won't do on its own
slides.body: Massage complements, rather than replaces, the other pieces: regular movement, desk breaks, sleep, hydration and managing stress. Relief is often short-lived unless some of those habits shift too.

slides.title: Three things to try today
slides.body: Set a reminder to roll your shoulders and look away from the screen every 30 minutes. Try a few gentle chin tucks. Put a warm pack on your upper shoulders for ten minutes in the evening.

slides.title: When to see your GP first
slides.body: A sudden severe headache, headache with fever or a stiff neck, confusion, vision changes, weakness, or a new pattern of headaches later in life need a medical check before massage. Uncommon, but important.

slides.headline: Tension sitting in your shoulders?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists at Hybrid Physiotherapy work on neck and shoulder tension and share simple habits to keep it settled between visits.

caption:
That dull band of pressure around your head by 3pm? Your neck and shoulders may be part of the story.

Tension-type headaches are often linked with tight, tender muscles in the neck, upper shoulders and base of the skull. Remedial massage can ease that tenderness, and research suggests it may reduce how often some people get these headaches. It works well as one piece of the puzzle, alongside desk breaks, movement, sleep and managing stress.

Some headaches need a GP first: sudden severe pain, fever or a stiff neck, confusion, vision changes, weakness, or a new pattern of headaches later in life.

Our remedial massage therapists tailor each session and give you simple habits for between visits. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: Using a Medicare chronic condition management plan for physio

slides.headline: Can Medicare help pay for physio?
slides.sub: How a GP chronic condition management plan works, step by step.

slides.title: The plan has a new name
slides.body: What used to be called an EPC or CDM plan is now the GP chronic condition management plan. It's for people with an ongoing health condition, and your GP decides whether you're eligible.

slides.title: Step 1: talk to your GP
slides.body: Your GP needs to set up the plan and refer you to allied health like physio. Mention you'd like physio included when you book, as it can take a longer appointment. We can't create the plan ourselves.

slides.title: What you can claim
slides.body: The plan can give a Medicare rebate for up to five allied health visits per calendar year. That's the total across services such as physio, chiro and others, not five of each.

slides.title: Expect a gap fee
slides.body: The rebate usually doesn't cover the full fee, so there's generally a gap to pay on the day. Ask our front desk about it before your first visit so there are no surprises.

slides.title: Making five visits count
slides.body: Use them for a thorough assessment, a clear home program and check-ins to progress it. Many people spread their visits across the year rather than using them all in one month.

slides.headline: Got your plan? Bring the referral
slides.body: Bring your GP referral and Medicare card to your first visit at Hybrid Physiotherapy. We'll assess, set goals and help you plan how to use your visits.

caption:
Did you know Medicare may help with the cost of physio?

If you have an ongoing health condition, your GP may set up a chronic condition management plan (what used to be called an EPC or CDM plan). It can give a Medicare rebate for up to five allied health visits per calendar year, shared across services like physio and chiro.

A few things to know: your GP needs to set it up and refer you, we can't create it ourselves, and there's usually a gap fee because the rebate doesn't cover the full cost. Ask our front desk about the gap before your first visit.

topic: Hamstring strain: getting back to sport safely

slides.headline: Hamstring strain: the road back to sport
slides.sub: What a sensible return usually looks like, stage by stage.

slides.title: First few days: calm, not still
slides.body: Ease off sprinting and hard stretching, but keep walking as comfort allows. Gentle movement and light muscle activation early on usually help more than complete rest or strapping yourself to the couch.

slides.title: Strength is the main event
slides.body: Progress from bridges and isometric holds to exercises that load the hamstring at longer lengths, like Romanian deadlifts and slider curls. Research suggests eccentric work such as Nordics can reduce repeat strains.

slides.title: Build running back gradually
slides.body: Start with easy jogging, then strides, then faster running over a couple of weeks. Increase one thing at a time: speed, distance or change of direction. A mild ache that settles overnight is usually fine.

slides.title: Signs you're ready to play
slides.body: Strength close to the other leg, sprinting at top speed without hesitation, and getting through full training sessions. Feeling fine walking around is not the same as being ready to sprint.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A loud pop, large bruising, pain right up near the sitting bone, or real trouble walking deserve a prompt assessment. Most strains don't need a scan, but these features are worth a proper look.

slides.headline: Want a plan for match day?
slides.body: Our Milton and Sunnybank physios assess the strain, set a staged return and test your strength and speed before you're back on the field.

caption:
Felt that grab in the back of your thigh mid-sprint? Here's what the road back usually looks like.

Most hamstring strains respond well to a staged plan. Keep walking early on, then build strength, with exercises that load the hamstring at longer lengths doing a lot of the heavy lifting. Running comes back gradually: easy jogging, strides, then faster efforts, changing one thing at a time.

Being ready to play means strength close to the other leg and sprinting flat out without hesitation, not just walking comfortably. A loud pop, large bruising, pain near the sitting bone or trouble walking are worth a prompt assessment.

topic: Morning back stiffness explained

slides.headline: Why is your back stiffest at 7am?
slides.sub: Morning stiffness is common. Here's what's usually going on.

slides.title: Overnight, you barely move
slides.body: Lying fairly still for hours means your joints and muscles haven't been loaded much. Discs also take on a little fluid overnight. It's usually normal for things to feel tight for the first little while.

slides.title: Why it eases as you move
slides.body: Movement warms tissues up and gets circulation going. That's why most people feel looser after a shower and a walk. Stiffness that settles within half an hour is typically the common, mechanical kind.

slides.title: Try a gentle wake-up routine
slides.body: Before getting up, do some slow knee rocks side to side and a few pelvic tilts. Then a warm shower and a five-minute walk. Go easy on heavy lifting or deep bending in the first hour.

slides.title: Where chiro fits in
slides.body: Our chiropractors may use joint mobilisation or adjustments to help you move more comfortably, alongside exercises and advice on sleep and activity. Adjustments are one tool, not the whole plan.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Stiffness that lasts well over 30 minutes most mornings, eases with exercise rather than rest, wakes you in the second half of the night, or comes with fever or weight loss deserves a GP check.

slides.headline: Tired of stiff mornings?
slides.body: Chat to our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy. We'll assess how your back moves and give you a simple routine to start your day.

caption:
Shuffling to the kettle like you've aged 30 years overnight?

Morning back stiffness is really common. You've barely moved for hours and your discs take on a little fluid overnight, so things often feel tight until you get going. Most people loosen up within half an hour of moving, and a warm shower and a short walk usually help.

Try slow knee rocks and pelvic tilts before you get out of bed, and go easy on heavy lifting for the first hour. Stiffness that lasts well beyond 30 minutes, eases with exercise rather than rest, or wakes you in the early hours is worth a GP check.

topic: Core strength myths

slides.headline: Core strength: four myths to drop
slides.sub: What clinical Pilates actually focuses on, and what it doesn't.

slides.title: Myth: a weak core causes back pain
slides.body: Research suggests the link is weaker than most people think. Plenty of people with strong abs get back pain, and plenty with average cores don't. Confidence, movement variety and overall strength often matter more.

slides.title: Myth: core means six-pack muscles
slides.body: Your core includes the deep abdominals, back muscles, diaphragm, pelvic floor and the muscles around your hips. They work together, so we train them together rather than chasing crunches.

slides.title: Myth: you must brace all day
slides.body: Constantly sucking in or bracing can make movement stiff and tiring. Most everyday tasks only need a light, automatic level of support. Save firmer bracing for heavier lifts at the gym.

slides.title: Myth: Pilates is just stretching
slides.body: Clinical Pilates is progressive strength training using mat work and equipment like the reformer. Springs add resistance or support, so sessions can be adjusted for a flare-up or built up for sport.

slides.title: Try this today: the dead bug
slides.body: Lie on your back with knees and arms up. Slowly lower the opposite arm and leg as you breathe out, keeping your lower back relaxed. Five slow reps each side is a good starting point.

slides.headline: Train your core the useful way
slides.body: Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy starts with an assessment, then builds a program around your goals, history and how you like to move.

caption:
"Just strengthen your core" might be the most overused advice in fitness.

Your core is more than your abs. It's a team of deep abdominals, back muscles, diaphragm, pelvic floor and hip muscles, and it tends to work well when it's trained as a team. Research suggests a "weak core" isn't the simple cause of back pain it's often made out to be, and bracing all day tends to make movement stiff rather than safe.

Clinical Pilates is progressive strength training, on the mat and the reformer, that can be adjusted for a flare-up or built up for sport. Try five slow dead bugs each side today as a starting point.

topic: Jaw clicking and TMJ pain: yes, physio can help

slides.headline: Jaw clicks and aches? Physio can help
slides.sub: Most jaw pain settles with simple, practical steps.

slides.title: Clicking on its own is common
slides.body: Lots of people have a jaw that clicks without any pain. If it's not sore and opens fully, it usually isn't a concern. Pain, locking or trouble opening are the things worth assessing.

slides.title: What often drives jaw pain
slides.body: Clenching or grinding, long stressful days, chewing gum, a forward head posture at the desk and tired jaw muscles. Often it's a mix, and it tends to fluctuate with stress and sleep.

slides.title: Easy things to try today
slides.body: Rest position: lips together, teeth apart, tongue resting on the roof of your mouth. Choose softer foods for a few days, skip the gum, and yawn gently with a hand under your chin.

slides.title: What a physio session involves
slides.body: An assessment of your jaw, neck and posture, gentle hands-on treatment to the jaw muscles, and exercises for controlled opening. We work alongside your dentist if a splint is part of the plan.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A jaw that locks open or closed, pain after a knock to the face, swelling, fever, or pain with numbness in the face should be seen promptly by your GP or dentist.

slides.headline: Sore jaw? Let's take a look
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your jaw, neck and posture together and give you a clear plan to follow at home.

caption:
Your jaw clicks every time you yawn. Should you worry?

Usually not. Lots of people have a jaw that clicks without pain. It's pain, locking or trouble opening that are worth getting assessed. Jaw pain is often linked to clenching or grinding, stressful days, chewing gum and long hours at a desk with your head poking forward.

Try this today: lips together, teeth apart, tongue resting on the roof of your mouth. Choose softer foods for a few days and skip the gum. If your jaw locks, swells, or hurts after a knock to the face, see your GP or dentist promptly.

topic: Pillows and sleep position for a sore neck

slides.headline: Which pillow for a sore neck?
slides.sub: There's no magic pillow. Here's what usually matters more.

slides.title: Aim for a neutral neck
slides.body: Whatever your position, your head should sit roughly in line with your spine, not propped up or dropping down. The right pillow height fills the gap between your head and the mattress.

slides.title: If you sleep on your side
slides.body: You'll usually need a firmer, higher pillow to fill the space above your shoulder. Hugging a pillow in front of you can stop you rolling forward and twisting your neck through the night.

slides.title: If you sleep on your back
slides.body: A thinner pillow usually works, so your chin isn't pushed down towards your chest. A small rolled towel inside the pillowcase can gently support the natural curve of your neck.

slides.title: Tummy sleeping and sore necks
slides.body: Lying on your front means turning your head fully to one side for hours, which often aggravates a sore neck. Try a very flat pillow, or gradually train yourself into side lying instead.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Neck pain with pins and needles or weakness in the arm, severe headaches, dizziness, fever, or pain after a fall or car accident should be checked by a health practitioner promptly.

slides.headline: Still waking up with a stiff neck?
slides.body: Our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy assess your neck and sleep setup, and combine hands-on care with simple exercises you can do at home.

caption:
Spent a small fortune on pillows and your neck still hates you in the morning?

There's no single perfect pillow. What matters is keeping your head roughly in line with your spine for your sleep position. Side sleepers usually need a firmer, higher pillow to fill the gap above the shoulder. Back sleepers often do better with a thinner one, maybe with a rolled towel inside the pillowcase. Tummy sleeping twists the neck for hours, so a very flat pillow or gradually shifting to your side can help.

Neck pain with arm pins and needles or weakness, severe headaches, dizziness or pain after a fall or accident should be checked promptly.

topic: How often should you get a remedial massage?

slides.headline: How often should you book a massage?
slides.sub: It depends on your goal. Here's a realistic guide.

slides.title: For a recent flare-up
slides.body: Many people find one or two sessions, about a week apart, help ease muscle tension while they get moving again. Massage tends to help most alongside exercises from your physio.

slides.title: For ongoing desk tension
slides.body: Every two to four weeks suits lots of office workers. Pair it with regular desk breaks and a few stretches, so the relief lasts longer between appointments rather than fading by Wednesday.

slides.title: For training and sport
slides.body: Around big training blocks or events, every two to three weeks is common. Avoid deep work in the day or two before a race. A lighter session afterwards can feel great.

slides.title: Signs you could space it out
slides.body: If tension stays settled between visits and you're managing well with your own routine, spreading sessions further apart makes sense. Massage complements active rehab, it doesn't replace it.

slides.title: Budget and health fund tips
slides.body: If your extras cover includes remedial massage, HICAPS lets you claim on the spot. Check your annual limit with your fund and plan your sessions around it across the year.

topic: Side hip pain when lying on it (gluteal tendinopathy)

slides.headline: Hip hurts when you lie on it?
slides.sub: Side hip pain is common and usually responds well to load changes.

slides.title: What's often going on
slides.body: Pain on the outside of the hip, tender to touch, worse lying on that side or climbing stairs, is often linked to the gluteal tendons. It's common from middle age, especially after a change in activity.

slides.title: Positions that often aggravate it
slides.body: Crossing your legs, hitching onto one hip, low chairs and glute stretches that pull the leg across your body. These can compress the tendons against the hip bone and keep them irritated.

slides.title: Sleep tweaks for tonight
slides.body: Lie on the other side with a pillow between your knees so your top leg doesn't drop across. Some people also find a softer mattress topper takes pressure off the sore side.

slides.title: Why strength work matters
slides.body: Current guidelines favour education and progressive strengthening, starting with gentle holds and building to exercises like bridges and step-ups. It's usually a gradual process over a few months.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Hip pain after a fall, pain deep in the groin, a limp that's getting worse, fever, or night pain that doesn't change with position should be assessed promptly by your GP or physio.

slides.headline: Want to sleep on that side again?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios work out what's driving the pain and build a strength program that fits around your week.

caption:
Can't lie on your side without your hip complaining?

Pain on the outside of the hip that's tender to touch and worse lying on it or climbing stairs is often linked to the gluteal tendons. It's common, and it usually responds well to changing how the tendons are loaded.

Tonight, try sleeping on the other side with a pillow between your knees. During the day, avoid crossing your legs, hitching onto one hip and deep glute stretches that pull the leg across your body. Current guidelines favour progressive strengthening, built up gradually over a few months. Pain after a fall, a worsening limp or fever should be checked promptly.

topic: Tight hips from desk work: a Pilates approach

slides.headline: Desk-day hips feeling locked up?
slides.sub: A Pilates-style approach to getting them moving again.

slides.title: Tight often means under-used
slides.body: Hours of sitting keeps your hips in one position. That feeling of tightness is often your body asking for movement and variety, rather than a sign that anything is stuck for good.

slides.title: Move through the full range
slides.body: Pilates works the hips through bending, straightening, rotating and moving out to the side, under control. Using the whole range regularly often eases that stuck feeling more than static stretching alone.

slides.title: Three moves for your lunch break
slides.body: Try ten standing leg swings each side, five slow half-kneeling hip stretches with a glute squeeze, and ten bridges. It takes about five minutes and needs no equipment at all.

slides.title: Strength helps hips feel looser
slides.body: Stronger glutes and hip muscles give your body the confidence to let go. Reformer work like footwork, side-lying leg presses and lunges builds strength while moving through range.

slides.title: Break up the sitting
slides.body: Stand up every 30 to 45 minutes, alternate sitting and standing if you can, and take phone calls on your feet. Small, frequent changes often matter more than one long session.

slides.headline: Want hips that move freely?
slides.body: Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy assesses how your hips move and builds a clinical Pilates program that fits around your work week.

Stand up after a long meeting and your hips feel about 80 years old?

Sitting keeps your hips in one position for hours, and that tight feeling is often your body asking for movement and variety. Pilates works the hips through their full range under control, and adds strength so your body feels confident to let go.

Try this at lunch: ten standing leg swings each side, five slow half-kneeling hip stretches with a glute squeeze, and ten bridges. Then stand up every 30 to 45 minutes and take calls on your feet. Small, frequent changes usually beat one big stretch session.

topic: Tight hip flexors from sitting: myth or real?

slides.headline: Tight hip flexors: myth or real?
slides.sub: What research suggests about sitting, and what actually helps.

slides.title: The short answer: partly myth
slides.body: Research suggests sitting doesn't usually shorten muscles in a lasting way. Many desk workers have normal hip flexor length when tested, yet still feel tight at the front of the hip.

slides.title: Why they still feel tight
slides.body: Feeling tight is a sensation, not a measurement. Staying in one position, low activity, tired muscles and stress can all make the front of the hip feel stiff, even when your range is fine.

slides.title: What tends to help more
slides.body: Moving often, walking breaks, and strengthening the hips and glutes. A short stretch can feel good, but variety of movement through the day usually makes a bigger difference over time.

slides.title: A quick desk-worker routine
slides.body: Every hour or so, stand up and do five slow lunges each side, ten bridges or glute squeezes, and a short walk around the office. Build up gradually and keep it comfortable.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Groin pain that catches with movement, clicking with sharp pain, a limp, pain at night, or pain after a fall or a big jump in training deserves a proper assessment.

slides.headline: Front of your hip still grumbling?
slides.body: Our Sunnybank and Milton physios assess how your hips move and handle load, then give you a practical plan that fits around desk work.

topic: Massage and recovery for weekend warriors

slides.headline: Sore Monday after a big Saturday?
slides.sub: Where massage fits in weekend recovery, and what matters more.

slides.title: Soreness after sport is normal
slides.body: Muscle soreness that peaks a day or two after unusual effort is common and usually settles within a few days. It's a sign you've done more than your body is used to, not an injury.

slides.title: Where massage can help
slides.body: Research suggests massage can reduce how sore you feel and help you feel more relaxed after hard exercise. It's a handy recovery tool, but it won't replace consistent training.

slides.title: Timing your massage
slides.body: A lighter session a day or two after your game or long ride often feels good. Leave deeper work until the soreness has eased, and skip it right before a big event.

slides.title: What matters more than massage
slides.body: Sleep, a decent meal with protein, fluids and some easy movement the next day. And train a little midweek, so Saturday isn't the only time your body works hard.

slides.title: When it's more than soreness
slides.body: Sharp pain during the activity, swelling, bruising, pain that isn't easing after a few days, or trouble bearing weight usually needs a physio assessment rather than a massage.

slides.headline: Recovery that fits your weekend
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists at Hybrid Physiotherapy tailor pressure to how you're feeling, and our physios are on hand if something needs a closer look.

topic: Chiro or physio? Why we work together

slides.headline: Chiro or physio? Honestly, often both
slides.sub: Why our chiropractors and physios work side by side.

slides.title: There's a lot of overlap
slides.body: Chiropractors and physiotherapists both assess muscles, joints and movement, and both use hands-on treatment and exercise. The differences are more about training background and preferred tools.

slides.title: What chiro sessions often include
slides.body: An assessment, spinal and joint adjustments or mobilisation, soft tissue work and home exercises. Adjustments are one tool that can help people move more comfortably, used alongside activity and advice.

slides.title: What physio sessions often include
slides.body: An assessment, hands-on treatment and a strong focus on progressive exercise and rehab, from recovering after an injury through to getting back to sport or work.

slides.title: Why working together helps
slides.body: Under one roof, we can refer between each other, share notes with your consent and blend approaches. You might see a chiropractor for a stiff back and a physio for your running program.

slides.title: How to choose where to start
slides.body: Start with whoever you feel comfortable with. If our team thinks another practitioner would suit your situation better, we'll tell you honestly and help organise it for you.

slides.headline: Not sure who to book?
slides.body: Call Hybrid Physiotherapy and tell us what's going on. We'll suggest a chiropractor or physio to start with, and work together from there.

topic: Thumb and wrist pain from phones and carrying babies

slides.headline: Sore thumb from phones or lifting bubs?
slides.sub: Why the base of the thumb gets grumpy, and what helps.

slides.title: A very common overload
slides.body: Pain at the base of the thumb or the thumb side of the wrist often builds when those tendons are loaded more than usual. New parents and heavy phone users see it a lot.

slides.title: The baby lift culprit
slides.body: Scooping a baby up under the arms with thumbs spread wide loads the thumb tendons hard. Try lifting with palms facing up, supporting under the bottom and head, and keep your wrists straight.

slides.title: Phone habits to change
slides.body: Hold your phone in both hands, scroll with your index finger, or prop it on a stand. Voice-to-text and a few shorter sessions instead of one long scroll can help as well.

slides.title: Settle it, then strengthen it
slides.body: Relative rest from painful movements, sometimes a supportive brace if advised, then gradual strengthening for the thumb and wrist. Most people improve over a few weeks with the right changes.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain after a fall onto the hand, swelling that isn't settling, numbness or tingling in the fingers, or weakness when gripping should be assessed promptly by your GP or physio.

slides.headline: Thumb still grumbling?
slides.body: Our Milton and Sunnybank physios assess your hand and wrist, show you easier ways to lift and hold, and give you a simple plan.

Thumb aching every time you pick up the baby or your phone?

topic: Returning to running after a break

slides.headline: Back to running after months off?
slides.sub: A gradual plan that respects what your body can handle right now.

slides.title: Start lower than you think
slides.body: Your heart and lungs often bounce back faster than your tendons and bones. A good starting point is walk-run intervals, like one minute jogging and two minutes walking, for 20 to 30 minutes.

slides.title: Build one thing at a time
slides.body: Increase time before pace. Add a little each week and run every second day at first. Every third or fourth week, hold steady or ease back slightly to let your body catch up.

slides.title: Use the next-morning test
slides.body: Mild soreness during a run that settles by the next morning is usually fine. Pain that's worse the next day, or changes how you run, means easing back to the previous step.

slides.title: Add strength twice a week
slides.body: Calf raises, split squats, bridges and step-ups build capacity for running. Two short sessions a week, around 20 minutes each, is a good starting point for most people.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain in one spot on a bone, pain that's worse each run, swelling, a limp or pain at night should be assessed before you keep building. Getting it checked early usually keeps the plan simpler.

slides.headline: Want a return-to-run plan?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios look at your strength and running history, then map out a gradual plan you can follow week by week.

caption:
Dusting off the runners after a long break? Your lungs might be keener than your legs.
